opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a funny story, because I went into that internship really excited. This was around the time when everyone thought self-driving was just a couple of years away, and Zoox was one of the most ambitious companies, building the whole vehicle from scratch. So I thought, this is where the frontier is.

But once I was inside, I realized that a lot of the day-to-day work wasn't the kind of research question I found most exciting. Autonomous driving at that stage was largely an engineering and systems-integration problem. You have a huge pipeline: perception, prediction, planning, control. Each piece is owned by a team, and progress comes from carefully grinding down the long tail of edge cases. That's incredibly important work, and I have a lot of respect for the people doing it. But I felt that the core intellectual question, how an agent should interact with the world, was being narrowed down a lot. A car mostly tries *not* to touch anything. Its whole job is to avoid contact.

What really drew me in, and what I ended up focusing on, was the opposite: physical interaction. How do you get a robot to pick things up, use tools, and manipulate objects in messy, unstructured environments? That felt much more open-ended to me. There wasn't a clear recipe yet, and learning, perception, and reasoning had to come together in a much deeper way. To me that's where the truly general intelligence question lives.

So I wouldn't say I lost interest in driving because it's unimportant. It's more that the internship helped me see what kind of problems energize me. I wanted to work on something where we didn't even know the right formulation yet, and robot manipulation was exactly that. In hindsight, it was one of the most useful internships I had, precisely because it showed me what I *didn't* want to spend the next ten years on.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous driving had become largely an engineering and systems-integration problem, but does not describe it as a 3D vision problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, I wouldn't say I lost interest in autonomous driving as a problem, I actually came out of that summer more impressed by it. What I lost was the sense that it was the right place for me to do research.

So I was at Zoox around 2017, working on perception and prediction stuff. And what you realize very quickly is that autonomous driving is a problem where ninety-five percent of the difficulty is in the last five percent. The core capabilities, detecting cars, following lanes, that all basically works. What doesn't work is the long tail. The construction zone with a guy waving a flag in some ambiguous way. The ball rolling into the street where you have to infer there's a kid behind it. And those cases don't get solved by a clever new model architecture. They get solved by enormous amounts of data, enormous amounts of engineering, very careful systems integration, and honestly a lot of patience.

That's fantastic engineering. It's just not research in the sense I wanted to do it. As a grad student, you want problems where a new idea can actually move the needle, where the bottleneck is understanding rather than scale. And in driving, the bottleneck felt like it was mostly scale and safety validation, which a PhD student with a couple of GPUs isn't going to meaningfully contribute to.

The other thing, and this is more personal, is that driving is a very constrained interaction with the world. You perceive, you predict, you plan a trajectory, but you never actually touch anything. You never manipulate anything. And I found myself much more drawn to robots that have to physically interact with their environment, pick things up, open drawers, deal with contact. That's where it felt like we fundamentally didn't understand how to do it yet, which to me is what makes a research problem exciting. So the internship kind of clarified what I wanted, almost by contrast. I'm grateful for it for that reason.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous-driving work was dominated by long-tail cases, data, engineering, integration, and safety validation; it does not say Danfei saw it as largely a 3D vision problem.

astra-6.text: What makes you say I lost interest in autonomous driving research after my internship at Zoox?

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helped me separate my interest in robotics from my interest in autonomous driving. There are really hard problems in driving, but in an industry setting, so much of the work is about making a particular system reliable—handling edge cases, integrating components, and testing everything very carefully.

That work is essential, but I realized that what excited me more was the open-ended question of how robots can learn new things and perform different tasks. So it wasn’t that I thought autonomous driving was uninteresting. The internship helped me understand which kinds of problems I wanted to spend my research career on.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the shift to preferring open-ended robot learning over system reliability work. It does not say autonomous-driving research had become largely a 3D vision problem.
